⚠ Safety first — read this before using any tool here

AllerGerald is an informational tool, not medical advice. It checks the words you type — it cannot see your kitchen, your suppliers, or your plate.

Always verify allergen information directly with restaurant staff before ordering or serving. Labels change, recipes change, and mistakes happen.

In an emergency, call emergency services (911 in Canada) and use an EpiPen if one is available. Do not wait, and do not rely on this page.

Tool 1

./ Allergen menu checker

Pick the allergens you are checking for, then type or paste a dish and its ingredients. Gerald scans the ingredient text for those allergens and their common hidden forms (whey = milk, tahini = sesame, and so on).

This checker only sees the text you enter. If an ingredient is missing from your list, it is missing from the result. Staff must always verify directly with the recipe and the product labels — this is not medical advice.

Tool 6 — free to read, no trial needed

./ Find-safe tips: eating out with allergies

For diners and families: what to ask before you book, and how to spot a kitchen that takes allergies seriously.

Questions to ask when you call ahead

  1. “Do you get many guests with food allergies? How do you handle them?”
  2. “Can I speak to the chef or manager about one dish, start to finish?”
  3. “Do you use a separate prep area, clean pans and fresh gloves for allergy orders?”
  4. “Is anything cooked in shared fryer oil?”
  5. “Can you check the actual ingredient label for me, not just the menu?”
  6. “If I come at a quieter time, is it easier for the kitchen to take extra care?”

Green flags — a kitchen that gets it

  • Staff ask you about allergies before you bring it up
  • The server writes the allergy down and repeats it back
  • The chef or manager comes to the table without being chased
  • They check labels instead of answering from memory
  • They say “we can't do that dish safely” when that's the truth

Red flags — slow down or walk away

  • “There's only a little bit in it” or “just pick it off”
  • Answers come instantly, with no label or recipe check
  • The allergy never gets written down anywhere
  • Staff seem annoyed by the question, or rush you
  • “We've never had a problem” offered as the whole safety plan

Trust the pattern, not one answer. And whatever a restaurant says: carry your EpiPen, and if symptoms start, call emergency services first and ask questions later.
